claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project.
Helm charts are directories of templated YAML manifests, a `values.yaml` file of default inputs, and metadata.
The `helm` CLI renders chart templates using Go template syntax and either installs the resulting manifests into a cluster as a release or prints them to stdout.
Helm charts are distributed through Helm repositories and indexed publicly on Artifact Hub.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
The Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
Pulumi is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
The Pulumi Registry includes providers for AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, Datadog, Cloudflare, GitHub, and Auth0.
Pulumi derives resource ordering from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready, and independent resources deploy in parallel.
Helm orders resources in a fixed order by Kubernetes kind (per kind_sorter.go in the Helm source).
Helm chart authors cannot declare dependencies between resources or subcharts, except through hook weights.
Helm stores release metadata as Secrets (or ConfigMaps) inside the target Kubernetes cluster.
Pulumi state is managed by Pulumi Cloud by default; self-managed backends include Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, and local files.
`helm rollback` restores a release to a previous revision recorded in release history.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack in a partially-updated state; `pulumi up` reconciles toward desired state and `pulumi refresh` detects drift.
The Helm SDK is available in Go only; other languages must shell out to the `helm` CLI.
Pulumi Automation API is a programmatic SDK in every supported language for embedding `up`, `preview`, and `destroy` in a host application.
Pulumi Policies is open source, with rules in Python, TypeScript, or Open Policy Agent Rego; Pulumi Cloud adds centralized policy management.
The Pulumi Enterprise edition adds Pulumi-maintained policy packs for CIS, PCI DSS, HITRUST, and NIST.
Helm has no native policy engine; policy is typically delegated to Kubernetes admission controllers such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper.
The Helm docs state: "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."

Helm's hardcoded kind order begins with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with any kind not on the list (including custom resources) last.
Helm uninstall runs the same kind-ordered list in reverse.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the API server in a single pass and doesn't wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.
In Helm, a subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind along with everything else, so chart dependencies don't control install order.
Helm chart hooks can be ordered with `helm.sh/hook-weight` annotations, and hook resources are not managed by Helm as part of the release.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts has been proposed in Helm HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output into another or setting the `dependsOn` resource option creates an edge in the dependency graph.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating resources that depend on it, and deploys independent resources in parallel.
Pulumi deletes follow the dependency graph in reverse.
Pulumi `helm.v4.Chart` supports the `config.kubernetes.io/depends-on` annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and `dependsOn` on the chart for dependencies on resources outside it.
Pulumi's dependency-ordered, parallel deployment makes updates faster than a strict serial sequence.
Pulumi Registry covers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and SaaS platforms like Datadog, Auth0, GitHub, and Cloudflare.
Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision.
Helm and Pulumi are commonly used in combination rather than as substitutes.
Two patterns cover most production deployments of Pulumi and Helm together.
Pulumi resolves chart values at deploy time and orders the chart install after the resources it depends on.
Pulumi resource outputs flow into a chart's `values` input as typed Pulumi outputs.
The FAQ section contains a heading "What's the difference between `helm.Chart` and `helm.Release`?" with anchor #whats-the-difference-between-helmchart-and-helmrelease.
Pulumi creates and deletes resources in dependency order, with each resource ready before dependents, rather than a fixed order by kind.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program is the most common adoption pattern.
Charts can be converted to native Pulumi code by rendering with `helm template` and converting the YAML with `pulumi convert --from kubernetes`.
`pulumi import` and the `import` resource option generate the corresponding code for imported resources.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider exposes Helm charts as first-class resources through `helm.v4.Chart` and `helm.v3.Release`; a program can pull charts from any Helm repository (public or private).

`helm.v4.Chart` renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object the chart produces as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
`helm.v3.Release` uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.

Helm merges objects from a chart and its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency doesn't make it install first.
Ordering within a Helm release requires chart hooks with hook weights or logic in the application itself.
